newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Assisted suicide sparks public row in Australia.
newsitem.headline: Assisted suicide sparks public row in Australia.

text.p: After a meal and a relaxing drink with his doctor on a warm Sunday afternoon, death came quietly to cancer sufferer Bob Dent in the world's first legal assisted suicide.

Dent's quiet death with family and friends in his home in this sleepy tropical town has ignited debate about whether "mercy killings" should be legal in some cases, or whether the dying should endure their agony until death comes naturally.

The government that runs this rugged and remote outback territory represents less than one percent of Australia's 18 million people, but its introduction of the world's first law legalising assisted suicide has far-reaching impact in Australia and overseas, say supporters and critics alike.

"This (death) clearly makes this a national debate," said government politician Kevin Andrews, sponsor of a private bill that would see the national parliament use its constitutional powers to over-ride the territory law.
"I don't think any longer can anyone say that this is something which simply affects the Northern Territory."
Dent himself fuelled the debate with an emotional plea from beyond the grave for Australia's parliament to reject Andrews and let the dying ease their pain and die with dignity.

In an open letter released on Thursday but written on the eve of his death by computer-delivered lethal injection, Dent said painkilling drugs given for his terminal prostate cancer made him suicidal.
"Drugs given to enhance the pain-relieving effects of the morphine have caused me to feel suicidal to the point that I would have blown my head off if I had had a gun," he wrote.

"The church and state should be kept separate. What right has anyone because of their own religious faith, to which I don't subscribe, to demand that I behave according to their rules and endure unnecessary intractable pain.

"If you disagree with voluntary euthanasia, then don't use it, but please don't deny the right to me to use it," wrote Dent, who in his final moments on Sunday told his doctor euthanasia was "an act of love".
While community and political leaders strongly condemn the law, a range of separate opinion polls show strong public support -- between seven and eight out of every 10 Australians.
Opponents, including political, aboriginal, medical, religious and other community leaders, say killing can never be legalised, warning abuse would follow and the weak would suffer.

Supporters, such as Dent's doctor and spearhead of the pro-euthansia campaign, Philip Nitschke, counter that people should be able to choose death for themselves when the pain gets too much, if they are still mentally sound.
Both sides agree the debate won't go away.
Andrews' challenge, backed by conservative Prime Minister John Howard, Labour opposition chief Kim Beazley and others, is due for parliamentary debate later this month.
A coalition of medical, religious and aboriginal groups is asking the country's peak court, the High Court, to declare the law unconstitutional.

Andrews, warning of the danger of abuse, said the debate was not about the individual's right to choose. "Once you have this legislation...it will be uncontrolled and subject to widespread abuse," he told reporters.

Church groups see the law as nothing more than legalised murder or suicide and moral decay. "I was, and still am, deeply ashamed that Australia should be the only country in the world to legalise the killing of an innocent person," Roman Catholic archbishop of Sydney Edward Clancy told reporters.
A politician from Howard's Liberal Party, Victorian state government leader Jeff Kennett, said euthanasia was beautiful.
"For people to be able to die with grace and dignity at their choosing, as opposed to suffering, is just beautiful.
"Life is about choice; death should be about choice and politicians ought to butt out," he said in a radio invterview.
The fate of Andrews' political challenge is uncertain.
While the government holds a strong majority, both sides of politics have agreed to free their members from party orders and allow them to vote according to their conscience.
One issue on which both sides agree is that Bob Dent's death on that warm Sunday afternoon won't be the last.
Nitschke, having convinced the necessary specialist and psychiatrist to support him once, believes he can do so again.
He has five more patients on his books seeking to die.
